docs.title: Welcome
docs.text: Nikita Bangiyev Datasheet as part of Fill-A-Bot for Team 201 Updated: November 9, 2026

docs.title: About
docs.text: This is my individual datasheet for EGR 304. It covers my part of our team project, the Main Control Board for Fill-A-Bot.

docs.title: Fill-A-Bot
docs.text:
Fill-A-Bot is our team's automatic water dispenser. You pick an amount, press start, and it fills your cup and stops by itself. Each of us builds one board, and the boards talk to each other over ribbon cables. Our team site is here.

  • Nikita Bangiyev: Main Control Board (me)
  • Cole Trask: flow sensing
  • Clay Belsher: pump control
  • Troy Reynolds: liquid amount sensing

It's meant for home kitchen use with plain drinking water, like getting a set amount of water for cooking, coffee, or a water bottle without a measuring cup. We picked kitchen use over lab use because a lab version would need cleaning, sterilization, and chemical safety rules we can't meet this semester. It isn't sterile and isn't meant for other liquids. There's more on this on our team's Product Requirements page.

docs.title: My Board
docs.text:
My board has the buttons and status LEDs the user sees, a light sensor that checks for a cup, and the Curiosity Nano that runs the fill. It tells Troy's board which preset was picked and tells Clay's board when to run the pump. Then it reads the weight status from Troy and the flow status from Cole, and stops the pump when the cup is full.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
The user presses UP for preset 1 or DOWN for preset 2, then presses START. My board sends the preset to Troy's board and tells Clay's board to run the pump. While it fills, my board watches the weight status from Troy and the flow status from Cole. When Troy's board says the target is reached, my board stops the pump. If Cole's board says there's no flow, it stops the pump and flashes the Fault LED. STOP cancels at any time.

A photoresistor under the cup spot goes through an op amp and a low-pass filter into the ADC, so the pump only starts when there's a cup. Three LEDs show Dispensing, Done, and Fault.

The boards don't use UART, I2C, or SPI. Each signal between boards is 2 plain wires, so it has 4 states (00, 01, 10, 11), and 00 is always the safe one.

docs.title: Ribbon Connectors
docs.text:
All three headers follow the class standard: 8 wires, pin 8 is ground, and no power pin. Pins 1-2 are my outputs and pins 3-4 come back from the teammate. My inputs have 100k pull-downs, so an unplugged cable reads 00.

Pin J1 (Cole) J2 (Clay) J3 (Troy) 1-2 Not used Pump command out Preset out 3-4 Flow status in Not used Weight status in 5-7 Not used Not used Not used 8 GND GND GND Signal 00 01 10 11 Pump command (to Clay) Stop Run Not used (stop) Not used (stop) Preset (to Troy) Preset 1 Preset 2 Preset 3 Preset 4 Weight status (from Troy) Not ready Below target Target reached Error Flow status (from Cole) No flow Flowing Not used (no flow) Sensor fault

Right now I only use Preset 1 (UP) and Preset 2 (DOWN). The other two codes are still there in case we add more presets.

docs.title: Component Selection
docs.text: These are the parts I picked for my Main Control Board. My teammates' parts are on their own pages. The parts I picked are in bold. The assignment says not to make tables for the microcontroller, buttons, LEDs, resistors, or capacitors, so those don't have one. Prices are DigiKey prices for one part from October 2026.

docs.title: 1. Power Source
docs.text:
Solution Pros Cons Option 1.Triad Magnetics WSU090-13009V 1.3A wall adapter$8.65/eachDigiKey / Datasheet - Most inexpensive adapter- In stock at DigiKey- Long 6 ft cord - Fine for my real load, but less than the regulator's 1.5A rating- Output can be off by 5%- Big body blocks the next outlet Option 2.MEAN WELL GST18U09-P1J9V 2A wall adapter$14.10/eachDigiKey / Datasheet - 2A is more than enough- Lowest ripple of the three- Wide temperature range - Most expensive adapter- Out of stock at DigiKey- Short 1.2 m cord Option 3.Triad Magnetics WSU090-20009V 2A wall adapter$12.43/eachDigiKey / Datasheet - 2A covers the regulator's full 1.5A- In stock at DigiKey- Long 6 ft cord - Costs more than the 1.3A one- Output can be off by 5%- Only rated up to 40 C

Choice: Option 3: Triad WSU090-2000 (Main Control Board)

Rationale: My board needs about 444mA from the adapter (432mA with the 25% margin, plus the regulator and the 9V LED), so all three would work. The class power budget template checks the adapter against the regulator's full 1.5A rating though, so I went with a 2A one. The Triad is in stock, costs less than the MEAN WELL, and has a 5.5 x 2.1 mm center-positive plug. The numbers are on my Power Budget page.

docs.title: 2. Barrel Jack
docs.text:
Solution Pros Cons Option 1.Same Sky PJ-102AHDC barrel jack, 2.0 mm pin, through hole$0.77/eachDigiKey / Datasheet - Rated 5A, way more than my board needs- Inexpensive- Lots in stock at DigiKey - 2.0 mm pin, so I have to check how tight the 2.1 mm plug fits- Right-angle part has to sit at the board edge- Costs a little more than the PJ-102A Option 2.Same Sky PJ-102ADC barrel jack, 2.0 mm pin, through hole$0.70/eachDigiKey / Datasheet - Most inexpensive jack- Same size and pins as the PJ-102AH- Lots in stock at DigiKey - Only rated 2.5A- Same 2.0 mm pin fit question- Less extra current room than the AH version Option 3.Switchcraft RAPC722XDC barrel jack, through hole$2.23/eachDigiKey / Datasheet - Rated 5A- Very common jack- Lots in stock at DigiKey - Most expensive jack, about 3x the others- Different footprint than the Same Sky jacks- No real advantage for my 0.44A load

Choice: Option 1: Same Sky PJ-102AH (Main Control Board)

Rationale: The class needs a barrel jack for the adapter. The PJ-102AH is rated 5A, which is way more than my 0.44A, and it's cheap. Its mating plug is listed as 5.5 x 2.0 mm and my adapter is 5.5 x 2.1 mm, so I'll check the fit when the parts come in.

docs.title: 3. 5V Linear Regulator
docs.text:
Solution Pros Cons Option 1.Texas Instruments LM7805CT/NOPB5V 1.5A, TO-220$1.86/eachDigiKey / Datasheet - Really common part- Built-in thermal protection- Easy to solder - Output can be 4.75 to 5.25V- About 2V dropout- Out of stock Option 2.STMicroelectronics L7805CV5V 1.5A, TO-220$1.08/eachDigiKey / Datasheet - Most inexpensive regulator- Lots in stock- Standard 7805 pinout - Output can be 4.75 to 5.25V- About 2V dropout- Gets just as hot as the others Option 3.Texas Instruments LM1086IT-5.0/NOPB5V 1.5A low dropout, TO-220$2.58/eachDigiKey / Datasheet - Output stays 4.9 to 5.1V- Only 1.5V max dropout- In stock at DigiKey - Needs an output cap with some ESR to stay stable (TI recommends 10uF tantalum or 50uF aluminum)- Different pinout than a 7805- Costs a little more

Choice: Option 3: TI LM1086IT-5.0/NOPB (Main Control Board)

Rationale: At the time my LCD backlight needed 4.9 to 5.1V, and the LM1086 was the only one here that stays in that range. The 7805s can go up to 5.25V.

Update (Rev 5): The LM1086 got backordered, so I switched to the ST LD1085V50 (DigiKey / Datasheet). It has the same TO-220 pinout and the same 4.9 to 5.1V output, it's rated for 3A, and my 10uF tantalum output cap still meets its 10uF minimum. The heat check below uses the LD1085V50.

docs.title: 4. Regulator Heat Sink
docs.text:
Solution Pros Cons Option 1.Same Sky HSE14-384225PTO-220 heat sink$2.24/eachDigiKey / Datasheet - 10 C/W at 1W in still air- Small 41.6 x 25 mm footprint- In stock at DigiKey - 38.1 mm tall- Needs an insulating pad since the LM1086 tab is at 5V- Not as strong as the Boyd parts Option 2.Boyd 529802B02500GTO-220 heat sink$2.02/eachDigiKey / Catalog - Lower thermal resistance (3.7 C/W at a 75 C rise)- Most inexpensive heat sink- Same size footprint - Out of stock at DigiKey- Also 38.1 mm tall- More cooling than I need Option 3.Boyd 530002B02500GTO-220 heat sink$4.03/eachDigiKey / Catalog - Lowest thermal resistance (2.6 C/W at a 75 C rise)- In stock at DigiKey- Same size footprint - 63.5 mm tall, hard to fit in a box- Most expensive heat sink- Way more cooling than I need

Choice: Option 1: Same Sky HSE14-384225P (Main Control Board)

Rationale: It's in stock, small, and enough to keep the regulator cool. The first Boyd is out of stock and the tall Boyd is way more than I need.

Heat check:

What Value Where it comes from Highest adapter voltage 9.45V 9V + 5% (Triad datasheet) Lowest regulator output 4.9V LD1085 datasheet Output current 432.3mA My power budget, with the 25% margin Regulator's own current 10mA max LD1085 datasheet Heat = (9.45 - 4.9) x 0.4323 + 9.45 x 0.010 2.06W Calculated Junction to case 3 C/W LD1085 datasheet (TO-220) Insulating pad 1.0 C/W My guess (a Bergquist SP900S pad is listed at 0.61 C/W) Heat sink 10 C/W HSE14-384225P datasheet (still air, 1W) Air inside the enclosure 40 C My assumption Junction temp = 40 + 2.06 x (3 + 1.0 + 10) about 69 C Calculated Limit 125 C LD1085 datasheet

So it stays well under the limit. I'll still check the real temperature once the board is built.

docs.title: 5. Cup Sensor (Analog)
docs.text:
Solution Pros Cons Option 1.Advanced Photonix PDV-P8103Photoresistor (LDR)$0.72/eachDigiKey / Datasheet - Big change between light and shadow- Sees normal room light- Used it in my photoresistor lab - Slow (about 60ms)- Room light changes the reading- Each one is a little different Option 2.Vishay TEPT4400Phototransistor$0.50/eachDigiKey / Datasheet - Most inexpensive sensor- Reacts quickly to changes- Responds like the human eye - Big part-to-part difference- Can max out in bright light- Narrow viewing angle Option 3.Vishay BPW34Photodiode$1.37/eachDigiKey / Datasheet - Output is very linear with light- Large sensing area- Reacts very quickly - Needs a different amp circuit- Also picks up infrared- Really small currents

Choice: Option 1: Advanced Photonix PDV-P8103 (Main Control Board)

Rationale: It's simple, cheap, and I already used it in lab. It sits under the cup spot with a 10k resistor, and the cup's shadow drops the voltage. A divider alone doesn't count as an analog sensor for this class, so it goes through the op amp below. I still need to test it with our real cups, since a clear cup might not make much of a shadow.

docs.title: 6. Op Amp
docs.text:
Solution Pros Cons Option 1.Microchip MCP6002-I/PDual op amp, 8-pin DIP$0.45/eachDigiKey / Datasheet - Rail-to-rail on 5V- Two op amps in one chip- Very low current - Higher offset voltage- Only 1MHz bandwidth- Doesn't quite reach the rails Option 2.Texas Instruments TLV2372IPDual op amp, 8-pin DIP$2.38/eachDigiKey / Datasheet - Rail-to-rail input and output- Wide supply range- 3MHz bandwidth - About 5x the price- Uses more current- Speed isn't needed Option 3.Texas Instruments OPA2340UADual op amp, SOIC-8$4.63/eachDigiKey / Datasheet - Lowest offset voltage- 5.5MHz bandwidth- Rail-to-rail on 5V - Most expensive op amp here- Surface mount is harder to solder- Uses the most current

Choice: Option 1: Microchip MCP6002-I/P (Main Control Board)

Rationale: A cup sensor doesn't need a fast op amp. The MCP6002 is cheap, comes in a DIP, and has two op amps in it. One buffers the LDR and the other has a gain of -3 around a 2.5V reference (10k in, 30k feedback). I'll set the cup threshold in code after testing.

docs.title: 7. Display
docs.text:
Solution Pros Cons Option 1.Lucky Light KW4-56NCUYA-P (Adafruit 811)4-digit 7-segment display$3.95/eachDigiKey / Datasheet - Big, easy to read digits- Bright in any lighting- Inexpensive for 4 digits - Can't show words like Ready or Filling- Can't show units- Needs a driver chip Option 2.Kingbright PDC54-11SURKWA2-character 14-segment display$5.60/each (need 4)DigiKey / Datasheet - Can show letters- Bright, high contrast- Big 0.53 in characters - 4 of them are too wide for my board- Needs a driver chip- Only 8 characters Option 3.Newhaven Display NHD-0216K1Z-FL-YBW16x2 character LCD$7.83/eachDigiKey / Datasheet - Shows the amount, units, and status at once- Built-in controller, no driver chip- Backlight makes it easy to read - Backlight uses up to 156mA- Needs a contrast pot- Uses 6 pins

Choice: Option 3: Newhaven NHD-0216K1Z-FL-YBW (Main Control Board)

Rationale: Our team requirements say the display has to show the amount, the units, and words like Ready and Filling, and the LCD was the only one that could do all of that.

Update (Rev 7): I took the LCD off my board in Rev 7, so my board doesn't have a display anymore. The status shows on three LEDs, and UP and DOWN pick preset 1 or preset 2.

docs.title: 8. Ribbon Cable Header
docs.text:
Solution Pros Cons Option 1.Wurth Elektronik 612008216212x4 box header, 2.54 mm$1.03/eachDigiKey / Datasheet - Most inexpensive header- Keying slot so the ribbon only goes in one way- Gold-plated contacts - No latch to lock the cable in- Shorter shroud than the 3M part- I need three of them (J1-J3) Option 2.3M N2508-6002-RB2x4 box header, 2.54 mm$2.31/eachDigiKey / Datasheet - Keyed so the cable only fits one way- Rated 5A per contact- Wide -55 to 105 C range - Most expensive header, about 2x the others- Fewer in stock- No latch to lock the cable in Option 3.Amphenol ICC 75869-132LF2x4 box header, 2.54 mm$1.10/eachDigiKey / Datasheet - Almost as inexpensive as the Wurth- Keyed so the cable only fits one way- Lots in stock at DigiKey - No latch to lock the cable in- Costs a little more than the Wurth- Datasheet link is from a distributor, not Amphenol

Choice: Option 1: Wurth Elektronik 61200821621 (Main Control Board)

Rationale: The class uses an 8-wire ribbon with a 2x4 connector, and I need three (J1 to Cole, J2 to Clay, J3 to Troy). The Wurth is the cheapest and it's keyed so the cable can't go in backwards.

docs.title: Pin Assignments
docs.text:

docs.title: Changes in Rev 7
docs.text: Rev 7 took the LCD (DS1), its socket (J7), and the contrast pot (RV1) off the board, along with J6, J9, the ribbon jumpers (JP3-JP11), R24, and C7, C14, C15, and C16. It added four 1N5817 diodes on the ribbon outputs (D7-D10, Vishay 1N5817-E3/53) and four 10k pull-downs (R30-R33, Yageo MFR-25FRF52-10K), and J5 is now a 2x5 header (Sullins PRPC005DAAN-RC). The table above is still what I ordered on Nov 4.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Prices are DigiKey prices from Oct 30, 2026, except the lines marked "Oct 25 price".
  • The LM1086 and the 30k resistor were out of stock on Oct 30. The LD1085V50 replaced the LM1086, and the 30k comes from Peralta stock.
  • The ribbon cables are shared by the team.

docs.title: Schematics
docs.text:
This is the schematic for my Main Control Board, Rev 7 (Nov 7, 2026). The PCB made from it is on my PCB page.

Figure 1: Main Control Board schematic, Rev 7

Files: Schematic PDF, Schematic image, KiCad project ZIP

docs.title: Power
docs.text: The barrel jack (J4) takes 9-12V, center positive. It goes through a T800mA fuse in a holder (F1) so it can be swapped, and then the LD1085V50 regulator (U2) makes 5V. C3 and C5 are on the input and the 10uF tantalum C4 is on the output, which is what the ST datasheet asks for. U2's tab is at 5V, so it gets an insulator on its heat sink. JP1 is between the regulator and the 5V rail so I can cut power or measure current. D6 lights up when fused VIN is on and D5 when 5V is on.

docs.title: Nano
docs.text: The Curiosity Nano gets 5V on VTG with VOFF tied to ground. C2 is its 0.1uF bypass cap.

docs.title: Buttons
docs.text: UP (RA0) picks preset 1, DOWN (RA1) picks preset 2, START (RA2) starts the fill, and STOP (RA3) cancels at any time. Each button has a 10k pull-up and a 10k/1uF RC debounce.

docs.title: Cup sensor
docs.text: The photoresistor sits under the cup spot and plugs into J8. U3A buffers it, U3B has a gain of -3 around a 2.5V reference from R6 and R7, and R10 and C9 make a low-pass filter (about 16 Hz) before the ADC on RA5. C6 is the op amp's bypass cap. JP2 can disconnect the ADC pin, and TP7, TP8, and TP9 are test points on the reference, the op amp output, and the ADC input.

docs.title: Status LEDs
docs.text: Dispensing (yellow, RD0), Done (green, RD1), and Fault (red, RD2). They're active low. There's no screen on the board anymore, so these LEDs are how the user sees what's going on.

docs.title: Ribbons
docs.text: J1, J2, and J3 go to Cole, Clay, and Troy. My four outputs go through 1N5817 diodes (D7-D10) with 10k pull-downs on the cable side (R30-R33), so a teammate's board can't push current back into my PIC. My four inputs have 100k pull-downs (R26-R29), so an unplugged cable reads 00 and the pump won't run. To cut off a teammate's board, I just unplug the cable.

docs.title: Debug and spare pins
docs.text:
D1 is the debug LED (RF2) and SW5 is the debug button (RF4). TP2-TP5 are on the power rails. J5 has +5V, GND, and 8 spare pins, and the other 14 spare pins go to test pads (TP18-TP31).

ERC shows 0 errors and 0 warnings, and every part I have to buy has its manufacturer part number in the KiCad file.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
The numbers are from our team's Product Requirements page.

docs.title: Power Budget
docs.text:
This checks that my 9V adapter and 5V regulator can run everything on my board at once, with a 25% safety margin. It only covers my board, since each teammate has their own adapter and regulator. I used the class template. Everything runs off 5V except the 9V power LED (D6), which is before the regulator.

I made this budget in Rev 5, when the board still had the 16x2 LCD. Rev 7 took the LCD off. The LCD lines below (logic, backlight, and contrast pot) add up to about 160mA, so the real Rev 7 current is a lot lower. The new 10k pull-downs on the ribbon outputs add less than 2mA.

My real draw from the adapter is 444.299mA (432.268mA, plus 10mA for the regulator, plus 2.031mA for the 9V LED), so there's lots of room left.

U2 is now the ST LD1085V50 because the LM1086 was backordered. I left the table as it was. The LD1085V50 is rated for 3A, so now the 2A adapter is the limit, and that still leaves about 1.5A.

docs.title: E. Battery Life
docs.text: N/A. My board runs off a wall adapter.

docs.title: Conclusions
docs.text:
The adapter and regulator can easily power everything with the 25% margin, and nothing comes out negative. The regulator turns about 2W into heat at this load, so it has a heat sink. With the LD1085V50 that keeps it around 69 C (the limit is 125 C).

Microchip only lists the PIC's max current at 3V, not 5V, so I used 170mA for the Nano to be safe. The real number should be a lot lower. I'll measure the board current through JP1 once it's built.

docs.title: PCB
docs.text:
This is the PCB for my Main Control Board (Rev 7, Nov 9, 2026). It's a 2-layer board, 100 x 100 mm with chamfered corners, made in KiCad 10 from my Rev 7 schematic.

Figure 1: PCB layout. Top traces are red, bottom traces are blue. The ground pours are hidden here so the traces are easier to see.

Figure 2: 3D view from KiCad

Figure 3: Top copper (left) and bottom copper (right) with the ground pours. The bottom is shown from underneath, so it's mirrored.

docs.title: Files
docs.text:
• KiCad project ZIP (Rev 7): schematic, PCB, my NB footprint library, symbols, and 3D models
  • Gerber files ZIP: top and bottom copper, solder mask, and silkscreen, the board outline, and the drill files
  • 1:1 print (PDF): top and bottom copper at actual size, for checking that the parts fit
  • DRC screenshot

docs.title: Design Rules
docs.text:
Rule Class rule My board Layers 2 2 Size 100 x 100 mm max 100 x 100 mm, 2 mm chamfers Copper 0.5 oz 0.5 oz Clearance 10 mil (0.254 mm) 0.254 mm Signal traces 15 mil (0.381 mm) min 0.381 mm Power traces 40 mil (1.016 mm) min 1.016 mm Annular ring 15 mil (0.381 mm) min 0.381 mm min Vias 19.7 mil (0.5 mm) drill 32 vias, 1.3 mm pad, 0.5 mm drill Copper to hole 10 mil (0.254 mm) 0.254 mm Hole to hole 31.5 mil (0.8 mm) 0.8 mm (closest pair is 1.06 mm) Solder mask clearance 5 mil (0.127 mm) 0.127 mm

I checked the power trace width with the IPC-2221 formula. A 40 mil trace in 0.5 oz copper can carry about 1.5A with a 10 C rise, and my fuse is only 800mA, so the power traces have lots of room. The 15 mil signal traces only carry a few mA.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
The power parts are in the top left corner. The barrel jack is on the left edge, the fuse is right next to it, and the regulator sits on its heat sink. Nothing is routed between the heat sink fins.

The Curiosity Nano plugs into a socket in the middle. Only the socket pads and their escape traces are under it. The three ribbon headers are on the top side along the right edge, so the cables all leave on one side and stay away from the buttons.

The buttons are in a row along the bottom edge where they're easy to reach (STOP, UP, DOWN, START from left to right). The status LEDs are in a row above the Nano. The cup sensor header (J8) is on the left edge, and the op amp and filter are below the Nano. J5 and the spare-pin test pads are right next to the Nano pins they connect to.

The bypass caps are close to their chips: C2 is 5.3 mm from the Nano's VTG pin, C6 is 3.8 mm from the op amp's power pin, and the regulator caps are 5 to 7 mm from U2.

docs.title: Ground and Routing
docs.text:
There are no ground traces. Ground is a copper pour on both sides with thermal reliefs and no islands, and all 49 ground pads connect through the pours. I didn't use the autorouter. Every bend is 45 degrees, and there are 32 vias. There's one T-junction left on FLOW_S1 near R26, because there's no room to move it without rerouting another signal.

"NB" is on the top copper in a big bold font (6 mm tall). "top" and "Fill-A-Bot Team 201" are on the top copper, and "bottom" and "Fill-A-Bot Team 201" are on the bottom copper, mirrored so they read right from underneath. My custom footprints have NB in them and are in my NB footprint library, which is in the KiCad ZIP.

docs.title: DRC
docs.text:
I ran DRC with "Refill all zones" and "Test for parity" turned on. It shows 0 errors, 0 unconnected items, and 0 parity problems. The 13 warnings are all silkscreen. The J1-J4 and HS1 outlines run to the board edge because those parts sit at the edge, and one LED outline is close to a test pad.

Figure 4: DRC results with the board in the same screenshot

docs.title: Changes After the First Layout
docs.text:
• Fixed sharp corners and T-junctions on BTN_START_N, +5V, VREF_2V5, and WT_S0, and closed a tiny gap on GPIO_RB0.
  • Made the NB on the top copper big and bold.
  • Added 3D models for the diodes (D7-D10) and J5.
  • Ran the Gerbers through the JLCPCB DFM check and cleaned up the silkscreen, so the labels sit inside their parts where they fit and none are on a pad or a via.
  • Set the solder mask clearance to 5 mil to match the class rules. That only changes the solder mask files.

docs.title: Ribbon Wiring for All Four Boards
docs.text:
Each signal between boards is 2 plain wires (4 states), and 00 is the safe default. The ribbon is straight through, so pin 1 on my header is pin 1 on the teammate's header. This is what each board has to wire to match mine.

Ribbon pin Cole (flow, J1) Clay (pump, J2) Troy (weight, J3) 1 Not used Pump command C1 in (from my RD4) Preset C1 in (from my RF6) 2 Not used Pump command C0 in (from my RD3) Preset C0 in (from my RF5) 3 Flow status S1 out (to my RC7) Not used Weight status S1 out (to my RE1) 4 Flow status S0 out (to my RC6) Not used Weight status S0 out (to my RE0) 5-7 Not used Not used Not used 8 GND GND GND

All boards use 5V logic. Every input has a 100k pull-down so an unplugged cable reads 00, and every output starts low at power-up. There's no power pin on the ribbon. My outputs go through a diode, so a high on my side shows up as about 4.7V.

docs.title: Main Board States
docs.text:
This is the plan for my firmware, based on Cole's flow chart. The timing numbers will get tuned on the real boards.

State Pump command Preset Waiting for Goes to Idle 00 (stop) Preset 1 or 2 UP picks preset 1, DOWN picks preset 2. START with a cup in place and weight status 01 Filling Filling 01 (run) Locked Weight status 10 Done No flow for 3 seconds, or flow status 11 Error STOP, or the cup is removed Cancel Error 00 (stop) Preset Fault LED flashes until STOP Idle Done 00 (stop) Preset Done LED stays on for 3 seconds Idle Cancel 00 (stop) Preset LEDs off for 1 second Idle

STOP cancels from any state, and a weight status of 11 (error) also goes to Error. A ribbon input only counts once it reads the same 3 times in a row (10 ms apart), so a read in the middle of a change gets ignored. The container weight is hard-coded on Troy's board for the demo.
